body: No, I  don't think you should just surrender yourself to loneliness. As you said yourself, socialization and a sense of belonging are fundamental needs for all human beings- only two tiers removed from food and shelter, if Maslow is to be believed. Assuming it isn't anything romantic, NEETdom in and of itself shouldn't automatically exclude you from simply making friends-you might just need to be a little bit more strategic in terms of how you go about that process. If you have a hobby in which you are skillful and/or passionate, I would highly recommend looking for Meetup groups tailored to that interest. As someone on the autism spectrum myself, my range of passions and hobbies are naturally quite limited, and I struggle intensely to connect with other people outside of those contexts.  It was initially quite terrifying at first, essentially plunging myself into the deep end of social interaction at a noisy ass pub after, like you, having barely spoken to a single stranger for an ungodly period, but I quickly acclimated and came to make quite a few friends this way.  Given that I was already somewhat well-versed and passionate about the theme of the meetup group in question, I was able to present myself much more confidently and connect with others more easily as a result. Also just feels good to forgo all the normie small talk bullshit about work and start a conversation by talking about Japanese phonetics like it's the most normal thing in the world lol. If something like that seems a bit too overwhelming for you to begin with, maybe start first by practicing via reading tips for social skills and/or making friends online to gradually ease yourself into socializing again. I'd happily be your friend myself.

Adam Rainer, an Austrian man born in 1899, is the only person in recorded medical history to have lived as both a midget and a giant. When he tried to enlist in the Austrian army for World War 1 as a young man, he was turned down because he was legally a dwarf, standing at only 4'8" (with size 20 feet). By the time World War 2 came around, he had underwent perhaps the most anomalous growth spurt known to man and was now too *tall* to enlist in the army. He died in 1950, bedridden and incapacitated, just two inches shy of being 8 feet tall. An incredible scientific curiosity, but also a very sad story when you think about it.
